title: A Silicon Qubit Gate That Misfires Once in a Million Tries
hook: Spin qubits in silicon just crossed 99.999% single-gate fidelity — and getting there meant discovering that some of the field's benchmark numbers were partly artefacts.
key_points: A spin qubit stores information in the spin of a single electron in a silicon device, and is driven with microwaves.
The relevant coherence metric under microwave driving is the spin-locking time T1rho, less studied than the free-evolution time T2*.
Removing nearby electron reservoirs from the device markedly lengthened T1rho, the key to the improvement.
The team also found that rectangular microwave pulses off-resonantly excite neighbouring qubits, creating substantial benchmarking artefacts under parity readout.
With spectrally tailored pulse shapes and cleaner device conditions they measured a pi/2 gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%.
The remaining error is dominated by incoherent noise rather than control imperfection.
content_html: Quantum computers need gates that almost never go wrong, because errors compound across a circuit. Spin qubits — single electron spins in silicon devices, appealing because they are small and made with semiconductor techniques — had already reached high single-gate fidelities, but not consistently, and the reason was murky. Most coherence work focuses on T2*, the time a spin stays coherent while left alone. Gates, though, happen while microwaves are hammering the spin.
extra_html: Kenta Takeda and colleagues went after that driven regime and reached single-qubit gate fidelities above 99.999%. Two things got them there. First, the device: they show that electron reservoirs sitting close to the qubit degrade the spin-locking coherence time T1rho, the metric that actually governs a driven gate, and that removing those reservoirs extends it substantially. Second, the measurement itself. In typical setups using parity readout and plain rectangular microwave pulses, the drive off-resonantly excites neighbouring qubits — which means part of what the field has been reporting as fidelity is a benchmarking artefact. With spectrally tailored pulse shaping to suppress that leakage, they measure a pi/2 gate fidelity of 99.99920(2)%, with the residual error dominated by incoherent noise rather than imperfect control. The paper reads as much as a set of practical guidelines — how to reach these fidelities and, just as importantly, how to verify them honestly — as a record.

related.title: Qubits and Quantum Computing
related.hook: A normal bit is a 0 or a 1. A qubit can be both at once — and linking many of them lets a quantum computer explore a staggering number of possibilities together.

related.title: For Quantum Computers, Colder Isn't Always Better
related.hook: The instinct is to chase ever-lower temperatures for quantum chips. A new study of real silicon qubits finds a 'sweet spot' instead, since cooling itself has a cost.

related.title: The Tiny Metal Islands Quietly Breaking Quantum Computers
related.hook: Quantum computers lose their fragile quantum states partly due to a decoherence source nobody had pinned down: stray metal islands from chip manufacturing acting like microscopic traffic jams.

flashcards.prompt: Why is T1rho the coherence time that matters for a driven spin qubit?
flashcards.back_html: Because gates are performed while microwaves are driving the spin. T1rho is the spin-locking coherence under that drive; T2* describes free evolution instead.

flashcards.prompt: What device change gave the largest coherence gain?

choices.text: Removing electron reservoirs sitting close to the qubit
Cooling the device by a further order of magnitude in temperature
Replacing silicon with a germanium quantum well

flashcards.explanation_html: Proximal reservoirs were degrading the spin-locking time T1rho; taking them away extended it dramatically and enabled the higher fidelity.

flashcards.prompt: What benchmarking artefact did the team uncover?
flashcards.back_html: Rectangular microwave pulses off-resonantly excite neighbouring qubits, which under parity readout distorts measured fidelities. Spectrally tailored pulses fix it.
